questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a frontal lobe function test?
questions.explanation: Frontal lobe tests include Stroop, Trail Making, Tower of London, Wisconsin Card Sorting, verbal fluency, Luria's motor tests, cognitive estimates, and multiple errands. The CVLT assesses verbal memory and is not specific to frontal lobe function.

questions.question_text: Aura is a commonly occurring phenomenon seen in which type of seizures?
questions.explanation: Auras are particularly common in temporal lobe complex partial epilepsy, generally lasting only a few seconds. They are stereotyped experiential phenomena preceding impaired consciousness.

questions.question_text: In a Broca's area lesion, which of the following features is seen?
questions.explanation: Patients with Broca's aphasia produce slow, halting, non-fluent speech, omit inflections and function words, and have impaired repetition. Comprehension, however, remains relatively preserved.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman began complaining of double vision and blurry vision 3 months ago and has since had diminishing interaction with her family, a paucity of thought and expression, and unsteadiness of gait. Her whole body appears to jump in the presence of a loud noise. An MRI scan and routine CSF examination are unremarkable. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The neurological complaints occurring early in the course of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease are often cerebellar or visual. Patients may complain of ataxia, clumsiness, or dysarthria, as well as diplopia, distorted vision, blurred vision, field defects, changes in colour perception, and visual agnosia.

questions.question_text: George is a 5-year-old boy with poor social interactions and stereotypical behaviours. Which part of the brain would you expect to be dysfunctional?
questions.explanation: This boy has features of autistic spectrum disorder. Hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis (involving to some extent the cerebellar hemispheres) is well-documented in autism. Purkinje cell count in the cerebellum is significantly lower in patients with autism.

questions.question_text: Which of the following structures are employed in processing emotionally salient memories?
questions.explanation: The amygdala and hippocampal complex, two medial temporal lobe structures, are linked to two independent memory systems. In emotional situations, the amygdala can modulate both the encoding and the storage of hippocampal-dependent memories.

questions.question_text: A gentleman presents with a 1-day history of sudden onset symptoms of akinetic mutism. What is the vascular origin of this presentation?
questions.explanation: Bilateral infarct involving the anterior cerebral artery produces quadriparesis (legs weaker than arms) and akinetic mutism (ventromedial or cingulate syndrome).

questions.question_text: Which of the following brain regions is associated with thermoregulation?
questions.explanation: The pre-optic area is a region of the hypothalamus responsible for thermoregulation. It receives input from receptors in the skin, mucous membranes, and hypothalamus.

questions.question_text: John is a 67-year old man admitted to the geriatric ward with a history of recent weight loss. On obtaining further history, he admits to loss of the sense of smell. This feature is suggestive of
questions.explanation: Anosmia is the inability to perceive odour. A permanent loss of smell may be caused by damage to the olfactory nerve or the frontal lobe areas that process smell, often after head injury or due to frontal tumours.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the precursor of serotonin?
questions.explanation: 5-hydroxytryptophan is the direct precursor to serotonin. Note that 5-hydroxytryptamine is serotonin itself.

questions.question_text: The somatodendritic inhibition of 5-HT release is regulated by
questions.explanation: The 5-HT1A receptor is found at both somatodendritic and post-synaptic sites. Somatodendritic 5-HT1A receptors in the dorsal and median  raphe nuclei are autoreceptors regulating 5-HT neuronal ring. Post-synaptic 5-HT1A receptors are found in the hippocampus and  periaqueductal grey matter where they regulate behaviours such as resilience, impulsivity and restraint of excessive response to stress. The  5-HT1A receptor may be an important target in the action of antidepressants. (Ref: Fundamentals of clinical psychopharmacology- 18)  The correct answer is: 5-HT1A receptors

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman awakens with inability to walk and is found on the floor by her family. Her examination shows right face, arm, and leg weakness and numbness. What is the most likely cause of her gait problems?
questions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided weakness indicates a left hemisphere infarction as the cause of her gait problem.

questions.question_text: Mr. P is a 77-year-old gentleman suffering from gradually progressive cognitive decline for last 6 months. He has history of Parkinson's disease for last 3 years and suffers from visual hallucinations. The chemical that is mainly involved and deficient in this condition is
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is Parkinson's disease dementia. In both Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease dementia, brain acetylcholine levels are  reduced similar to Alzheimer's disease. Therefore acetylcholinesterases (Anti-dementia drugs) could be used in the treatment of Lewy body  dementia.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y was diagnosed with HIV almost 2 years ago. He is now presenting with cognitive impairment. Which of the following cells is least likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: Although theoretically all CNS cells can be infected by HIV-1, most studies indicate an absence of in vivo infection in neurons.

questions.question_text: Regional cerebral blood flow is affected in schizophrenia. Which of the following area is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: Hypofrontality has been repeatedly demonstrated.  In schizophrenia:  Hypoperfusion: frontal lobes and frontal cortex, anterior and medial cingulate gyri, and parietal lobes.  Hyperperfusion: cerebellum, brainstem and thalamus.

questions.question_text: The post-mortem examination done on an elderly gentleman who suffered from a slowly progressive non-amnesic cognitive impairment, disinhibition and pill-rolling tremors reveals ubiquitin inclusions. Which one among the following genes is most likely to reveal a mutation?
questions.explanation: This is a case of frontotemporal dementia (FTD). FTD is caused by mutations in progranulin (PGRN) especially in familial FTD. PGRN is located  on chromosome 17q21.31.

questions.question_text: The density of D2 receptors seen in children before 5 years of age is greater than adult levels. Their regression to adult levels is reached during the second decade. The developmental process through which this is achieved is called
questions.explanation: Synaptic pruning refers to the natural elimination of unnecessary synapses that normally occurs in adolescence, making the brain more organised and efficient.

questions.question_text: A disturbance in cerebral torque is proposed as the underlying pathological change in which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation: 'Cerebral torque' refers to opposing right-left asymmetries of frontal and parieto-occipital regions of the brain.  Crow's hypothesis and observations suggest that a primary disturbance in psychosis is in brain structure, and this is related to cerebral  asymmetry in the form of torque.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common opportunistic infection of CNS in patients with AIDS?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmic encephalitis (TE) is caused by the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. The disease occurs almost exclusively because of reactivation  of latent tissue cysts. Primary infection occasionally is associated with acute cerebral or disseminated disease. Seroprevalence varies  substantially among di erent communities (e.g., approximately 15% in the United States and 50%--75% in certain European countries). Prior  to the introduction of antiretroviral drugs, the 12-month incidence of TE was approximately 33%. The incidence has decreased substantially  with the initiation of ART. Clinical disease is rare among patients with CD4+ T lymphocyte counts more than 200 cells/µL. Primary infection  occurs after eating undercooked meat containing tissue cysts or ingestion of oocysts that have been shed in cat feces and have sporulated  in the environment (which requires at least 24 hours). No transmission of the organism occurs by person-to-person contact (Retrieved from  http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr58e324a1.htm).  The correct answer is: Toxoplasma gondii

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist?
questions.explanation: Mifepristone is a type 2 glucocorticoid and progesterone receptor antagonist shown to ameliorate symptoms of major depression.

questions.question_text: The EEG findings of a patient shows multiple spike and wave activity. Identify the disease.
questions.explanation: Myoclonic epilepsy commonly shows rapid spike–wave and polyspike–wave activity on EEG.

questions.question_text: The substance that is secreted by hypothalamus and enhances food intake is
questions.explanation: Neuropeptide Y potently induces an increase in food intake and simultaneously stimulates vasopressin secretion.

questions.question_text: There is increased concentration in axon terminal prior to depolarisation with which of the following ions?
questions.explanation: There is a negative resting membrane potential of around -70mV. It is maintained by the sodium pump, which actively transports sodium  ions out of the cell and potassium ions into the cell. There is increased concentration of potassium ions in axon terminal prior to  depolarization. An action potential is propagated by the depolarization spreading laterally to adjacent parts of the neurone. An action  potential is initiated in the axon hillock when the synaptic signals received by the dendrites and soma are su cient to raise the intracellular  potential from -70 mV to the threshold potential of - 55mV. When this potential is reached, the Na+ channels present in the axon initial  segment will open. This Na+ inux causes a rapid reversal of the membrane potential from -90 to +40 mV. When the membrane potential  reaches +40mV, the Na+ channels close and the voltage-gated K+ channels open. K+ ions move out of the axon, and 'repolarizes' the  membrane

questions.question_text: Which of the following is least likely to be correct with regard to REM latency and depression?

options.text: REM sleep latency reduction precedes onset of major depressive disorder
Shortened REM latency is specific to depression
Relatives of depressed patients have increased prevalence of short REM latency
Reduced REM latency could persist even after successful treatment of depressive episode
REM latency reduction predicts higher relapse risk

correct_answer.text: Shortened REM latency is specific to depression

correct_answers.text: Shortened REM latency is specific to depression

questions.explanation: Short REM latency is associated with increased risk of major depression beyond the familial risk associated with a depressed proband.  Consistent with other heritable traits, both REM latency reduction and Slow Wave Sleep abnormalities have been observed preceding a rst  episode of depression in patients. But it has low predictive value as substantial number of those who have short REM latency, do not  develop depression. Short REM latency is not speci c to depression; it may be seen in PTSD, schizophrenia, eating disorders, etc  The correct answer is: Shortened REM latency is speci c to depression

questions.question_text: Mr. P, a patient attending your clinic, was started on clozapine a few weeks ago. He now complains of shortness of breath, tachycardia and fever. Which of the following would you request urgently?
questions.explanation: The most important consideration is clozapine-induced myocarditis. It occurs within 6-8 weeks of starting clozapine (median 3 weeks).  Symptoms include fever, tachycardia, u-like symptoms, fatigue, dyspnea (with increased respiratory rate) and chest pain. One proposed  monitoring protocol recommends obtaining baseline troponin I/T, C-reactive protein and echocardiography, and monitoring troponin and C  reactive protein on days 7, 14, 21 and 28. At least twice the upper limit of normal troponin was found in 90% of cases. In addition, persistent  abnormally high heart rate or signs or symptoms consistent with infective illness should be followed by daily troponin and C-reactive protein  investigation until features resolve. Ref: Ronaldson et al., Aust N Z J Psychiatry. 2011 Jun;45(6):458-65.  http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21524186

questions.question_text: Prolonged QTc interval is associated with:
questions.explanation: Methadone alone or combined with other arrythmogenic agents may increase the likelihood of QT interval prolongation, which is associated  with torsades de pointes and can be fatal. ECG monitoring is therefore recommended whilst taking methadone.

questions.question_text: Sally has a diagnosis of schizophrenia and is currently taking risperidone tablets. Her prolactin level tested recently shows an elevation that is twice the value recorded prior to commencing the treatment. Which of the following drugs could be considered as the best possible add-on treatment?
questions.explanation: For most patients with symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia, a switch to non-prolactin elevating drug is the rst choice. An alternative with  modest but evolving evidence is to add aripiprazole to existing treatment. Hyperprolactinaemia and related symptoms are reported to  improve fairly promptly following the addition of aripiprazole. Ref: Mir et al., Psychopharmacol. 2008 May;22(3):244-53

questions.question_text: A 47-year-old man developed seizures on taking an antipsychotic medication. The psychiatrist treating him initially reduced the dose of his antipsychotic, and later started him on sodium valproate. Which of the following antipsychotic drugs is most likely to produce this effect?
questions.explanation: Seizures may occur at any time whilst taking clozapine. It is a dose and plasma level-related e ect. Prophylactic valproate or lamotrigine is  used in high-risk subjects when titrating to a high dose of clozapine. EEG abnormalities are common in those on clozapine treatment; these  abnormalities do not always indicate seizure activity

questions.question_text: Mr. P developed cardiomyopathy on taking this medication for the last 9 months. The most likely drug is
questions.explanation: Clozapine is associated with myocarditis and cardiomyopathy. Myocarditis seems to occur within 6-8 weeks of starting clozapine (median 3  weeks) and cardiomyopathy may occur later in treatment (median 9 months) but both may occur at anytime.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is a risk factor for SSRI induced hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation: Risk factors for SSRI induced hyponatraemia include old age, female sex, low body weight, low baseline sodium concentration, history of  hyponatraemia, warm weather, reduced renal function, medical co-morbidity and some drug treatments like carbamazepine, antipsychotics,  thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, cancer chemotherapy and drugs like tramadol, omeprazole and trimethoprim.

questions.question_text: Sally has depression but would accept her treatment only if the probability of drug induced weight gain is low. Which of the following antidepressants is best to avoid?
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine is associated with weight gain in around 1/5th of subjects, especially in the rst 4 weeks of treatment. This e ect may be  secondary to its e ects on the 5-HT2C and H1 receptors

questions.question_text: Which of the following is primarily tested by using Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS)?
questions.explanation: The AIMS records the occurrence of tardive dyskinesia (TD) in patients receiving neuroleptic medications. This test is used to detect TD and  to follow the severity of a patient's TD over time.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the least likely feature associated with Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
questions.explanation: Bradycardia is not a feature seen in patients with NMS. The symptoms and signs of NMS include hyperthermia, rigidity, agitation, altered  levels of consciousness, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypertension, tremor, diaphoresis, raised CPK levels, leukocytosis and metabolic acidosis

questions.question_text: The upper normal value of QTc in females is
questions.explanation: The upper normal value of QTc in males is 440 msec and females is 470 msec. Mounting evidence links QTc values over 500 msec to a clearly  increased risk of arrhythmia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs increases the incidence of cleft palate when used in pregnant women?
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine increases the incidence of cleft palate. There are some anecdotal reports linking valproate and diazepam as well to this  abnormality.

questions.question_text: Which class of antidepressants, when used during pregnancy increases the risk of cleft lip/cleft palate in the newborn?
questions.explanation: Existing research evidence has shown a connection between prenatal use of SSRI anti-depressants and the subsequent formation of birth  defects like cleft lip and palate. In 2006, a Danish population-based cohort study published in Epidemiology reported that women taking SSRI  antidepressants from 30 days before conception to the end of the rst trimester were more likely to give birth to babies with congenital  formations, which may include cleft lip and palate.

questions.question_text: Which of the following adverse effects has not been reported in association with therapeutic doses of SSRIs?
questions.explanation: Several published reports of SSRI-induced movement disorders are available; they mostly report akathisia, dyskinesia, parkinsonism and  occasionally dystonia and bruxism. Most of these were reported when using normal therapeutic doses. SSRIs, especially escitalopram and  paroxetine, are occasionally associated with galactorrhea. Though rare, photosensitivity and hallucinations have been anecdotally reported  with SSRIs. Nevertheless, therapeutic range of SSRI dose is not associated with systemic hypertension, though SNRIs such as venlafaxine  carries this risk especially above the dose of 225mg/day.

questions.question_text: Which of these drugs is likely to cause tricuspid valve displacement towards the apex of the right ventricle in the newborn, when used during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Ebstein's anomaly is a congenital heart defect in which the tricuspid valves are displaced towards the apex of the right ventricle. Lithium use  has a well-known association with this cardiac malformation (relative risk is 10-20 times more than control). Some case reports have also  implicated benzodiazepines, although this is rare.

questions.question_text: The risk of developing seizures with the use of clozapine is increased by:
questions.explanation: Patients can have generalized tonic-clonic seizures during treatment with clozapine. Life-table analysis predicts a cumulative 10% risk of  seizures after 3.8 years of treatment. Clozapine-related seizures appear to be dose-related. High-dose therapy (greater than or equal to 600  mg/day) was associated with a greater risk of seizures (4.4%) than medium (300 to 600 mg/day; 2.7%) or low doses (less than 300 mg/day;  1.0%). Also, rapid upward titration may increase seizure risk. Ref: Devinsky O, Honigfeld G, Patin J. Clozapine-related seizures. Neurology.  1991 Mar 1;41(3):369)

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidementia drugs undergo breakdown by cholinesterase itself with no hepatic involvement in metabolism?
questions.explanation: Rivastigmine is metabolised by cholinesterase enzymes and undergoes no significant hepatic metabolism.

questions.question_text: Phenelzine has been shown to be superior to placebo in the treatment of
questions.explanation: The monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) have shown superior e cacy to other antidepressants in the the treatment of generalized social  phobia. Phenelzine in particular, has extensive placebo-controlled trial evidence in support of its use in social anxiety with nearly 67%  patients showing signi cant improvement during acute treatment.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following statements about atypical antipsychotic drugs is incorrect?

options.text: Atypical antipsychotics have relatively high serotonin HT-2A to dopamine D-2 receptor binding ratios
The extrapyramidal safety of atypical antipsychotics depends on the affinity for nigrostriatal dopamine D-2 receptors
High 5-HT2A:D2 ratios may underlie efficacy and safety advantages
Atypical antipsychotics have less affinity for nigrostriatal than typical antipsychotics
The efficacy of antipsychotic drugs appears to be determined by the affinity for nigrostriatal dopamine receptors

correct_answer.text: The efficacy of antipsychotic drugs appears to be determined by the affinity for nigrostriatal dopamine receptors

correct_answers.text: The efficacy of antipsychotic drugs appears to be determined by the affinity for nigrostriatal dopamine receptors

questions.explanation: The e cacy of antipsychotic drugs appears to be determined by the a nity for mesolimbic dopamine receptors and not by the a nity for  nigrostriatal receptors.

questions.question_text: Which of the following mood stabilisers is not recommended for prophylaxis of bipolar affective disorder?
questions.explanation: There is insufficient trial evidence to recommend topiramate for bipolar prophylaxis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a prodrug whose metabolite is used as an individual compound therapeutically?
questions.explanation: Paliperidone is 9-OH-risperidone.  Citalopram is not a prodrug - escitalopram is the therapeutically active S-enantiomer of citalopram.

questions.question_text: Which antipsychotic has a longer therapeutic effect attributable to its active metabolite?
questions.explanation: The apparent half-life of risperidone is 3 hours while the apparent half-life of 9-hydroxyrisperidone (also known as paliperidone) is about 21  hours (in extensive metabolizers). The pharmacokinetics of risperidone and 9-hydroxyrisperidone combined, after single and multiple doses,  were similar in extensive and poor metabolizers, with an overall mean elimination half-life of about 20 hours (RISPERDAL M-TAB - Food and  Drug Administration, http://www.fda.gov/ohrms/dockets/dockets/06p0245/06P-0245-EC1-Attach-1.pdf ).

questions.question_text: Which of the following measures can help reduce lithium-induced tremors?

options.text: Change time of administration to mornings only

questions.explanation: Administering lithium in smaller, more frequent doses reduces peak levels and tremors. Propranolol may also help.

questions.question_text: A psychiatric trainee has started lamotrigine in addition to a second mood stabiliser for a lady with a relapse of bipolar affective disorder. The second mood stabiliser is most likely to be
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate can inhibit the breakdown of lamotrigine and so can result in higher plasma levels of lamotrigine. Valproate also increases  the risk of allergic rash seen with lamotrigine.

questions.question_text: Mr Julian Andrews is a 32-year-old man who has presented with symptoms of low mood, lack of enjoyment, poor sleep, low energy levels and diminished appetite. How long would he need to have these symptoms before he could be diagnosed with a depressive episode under ICD-10 criteria?
questions.explanation: ICD-10 requires a person to have depressive symptoms most days, most of the time for at least 2 weeks before an episode of depression  can be diagnosed.

questions.question_text: Robin Wells is a 35-year-old who has recently been diagnosed with rapid cycling bipolar affective disorder. Which of the following is true about this disorder?

options.text: At least four episodes of bipolar disorder in 1 year
At least two episodes of bipolar disorder in 1 year

correct_answer.text: At least four episodes of bipolar disorder in 1 year

correct_answers.text: At least four episodes of bipolar disorder in 1 year

questions.explanation: Rapid cycling is defined by 4 or more mood episodes (manic, hypomanic, mixed, or depressive) within 12 months.

questions.question_text: The Sally Anne Test is a psychological test used with children. Which of the following is TRUE regarding the Sally Anne Test?

options.text: It is correctly interpreted by the age of 3
Girls are more likely to correctly interpret the test than boys
It is a test of second-order false belief tasks
It is a test of theory of mind

correct_answer.text: It is a test of theory of mind

correct_answers.text: It is a test of theory of mind

questions.explanation: The Sally Anne test is a test of theory of mind whereby children observe a scenario in which a doll (Anne) removes a marble from another  doll's (Sally's) basket and places it in a box. The other doll then enters the scene and the children are asked where it will look for its marble.  To pass the children must identify that Sally will look in her basket as she does not know that the marble has been moved. Children  generally pass it after the age of 4

questions.question_text: Siobhan Gibbons is a 72-year-old woman who was admitted following a fall. On examination she appears confused, is ataxic and nystagmus is present. She has a long history of alcohol dependence. During her stay her confusion becomes less prominent but her cognitive impairment remains. Which of the following statements about Korsakoff syndrome is NOT true?

options.text: Thiamine acts as a co-factor for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Reductions in thiamine-dependent enzymes lead to impairment of oxidative metabolism
Chronic severe thiamine deficiency results in insufficient concentrations to cross the blood-brain barrier
Reductions in thiamine pyrophosphate-dependent enzymes have been found in autopsied cerebellar vermis samples
Once the features of Korsakoff have been recognised, they can be reversed using IV Thiamine

correct_answer.text: Once the features of Korsakoff have been recognised, they can be reversed using IV Thiamine

correct_answers.text: Once the features of Korsakoff have been recognised, they can be reversed using IV Thiamine

questions.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome is irreversible. Early IV thiamine can prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy, but established Korsakoff deficits do not fully reverse.

questions.question_text: Mrs Delia Faber is a 40-year-old woman with a diagnosis of acute intermittent porphyria. Which of the following is FALSE about acute intermittent porphyria?

options.text: Physical signs often include an abdominal rash
It is an autosomal dominant disorder
It can be precipitated by use of clonazepam
Psychiatric side effects often include psychosis

correct_answer.text: Physical signs often include an abdominal rash

correct_answers.text: Physical signs often include an abdominal rash

questions.explanation: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is not typical characterised by a rash; abdominal pain is the most common symptom. It is usually inherited in  an autosomal dominant manner but autosomal recessive inheritance has been described. It is caused by mutations in the HMBS gene,  which codes for the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase. It causes acute attacks of abdominal pain and other symptoms, potentially  including psychosis. It can be precipitated by the use of medications, including clonazepam, alcohol, low carbohydrate diet, infections and  hormone changes during the menstrual cycle. A high-carbohydrate (10% glucose) infusion is recommended, which may aid in recovery.  Hematin and heme arginate is the treatment of choice during an acute attack. Heme is not a curative treatment, but can shorten attacks and  reduce the intensity of an attack

questions.question_text: Mr Daniel Banner is a 28-year-old man who has autoscopic hallucinations. Which of the following is TRUE about this phenomenon?

options.text: It describes altered perception of colour
It is seen only in depression
It is seeing oneself in one's external space
It is a normal clinical phenomenon

correct_answer.text: It is seeing oneself in one's external space

correct_answers.text: It is seeing oneself in one's external space

questions.explanation: An autoscopic hallucination is a visual misperception in which an individual sees himself or herself as if they are an external stimulus.

questions.question_text: Ron Hyke was subject to a traumatic brain injury following a collision between his car and another vehicle, two-and-a-half years ago. Following a period spent in a coma, he gradually recovered normal functioning in most domains. However, his partner feels that Ron's personality isn't what it used to be. He doesn't have the same humour or interests, he's more predisposed to being emotional, sometimes angry. Which of the following psychological tests would you consider appropriate in testing Ron for post-traumatic personality changes?
questions.explanation: The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) is a standardised psychometric test which has been used to test personality change  and has some validity in cases of post-traumatic brain injury

questions.question_text: Mrs Brown is attending the memory clinic and undergoing cognitive testing for suspected Alzheimer's dementia. During one part of the examination the psychologist reads a list of 10 words. After 20 minutes and other tasks Mrs Brown is asked to recall as many words as possible. This is an example of testing
questions.explanation: Delayed recall involves the retrieval of previously encoded words, whereas delayed recognition measures only whether or not a word has  been encoded and consolidated.   Tests of free recall involve immediate assessment of what is recalled after a list is read e.g. upon hearing the list read, patients are instructed  that they will be asked to repeat as many words as they can.  Reading a list of words followed by a 20-minute delay and asking the patient to recall as many words as possible tests 'delayed recall'.   Asking the patient to point out whether a given word was in the original list after a delay is testing 'delayed recognition' as well as  consolidation. Semantic memory refers to general world knowledge accumulated through the lifespan.

questions.question_text: According to ICD-10, how long must symptoms be present for before a diagnosis of mania can be made?
questions.explanation: ICD-10 requires manic symptoms to be present for at least 7 consecutive days to diagnose a manic episode.

questions.question_text: Ms Coyle describes her 18-month-old son Thomas. He is not upset when left alone to play, is calm with unfamiliar visitors, and does not notice his mother’s return or make eye contact. According to Ainsworth’s attachment types, Thomas’s behaviour is best described as:
questions.explanation: Avoidant attachment is marked by emotional distance and lack of distress or recognition on the caregiver’s return.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a DSM-IV Cluster C personality disorder?
questions.explanation: The cluster C personality disorders in DSM-IV are dependent, anxious-avoidant and anankastic (obsessive-compulsive).

questions.question_text: Susan Miers is a 25-year-old woman with an IQ of 36. How severe is her degree of learning disability?
questions.explanation: A classi cation of mild, moderate, severe and profound has been used to describe the degree of learning disability. IQ measurement has  traditionally been used to de ne severity:   • Profound - IQ of less than 20   • Severe - IQ of 20-34   • Moderate - IQ of 35-49   • Mild - IQ of 50-70  The correct answer is: Moderate mental retardation

questions.question_text: Which personality disorder is included in DSM-IV but NOT classified as a personality disorder in ICD-10?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization's ICD-10 uses the name schizotypal disorder. It is classi ed as a clinical disorder associated with  schizophrenia, rather than a personality disorder as in DSM-5

questions.question_text: Graham describes his partner Sharon. Which description is NOT part of the ICD-10 criteria for histrionic personality disorder?

options.text: Her emotions fluctuate rapidly and can appear shallow
She often wears revealing, sexually provocative clothing
She appears not to mind whether she is praised or criticised
She is easily influenced by others
At a party, she talks loudly and must be the centre of attention

correct_answer.text: She appears not to mind whether she is praised or criticised

correct_answers.text: She appears not to mind whether she is praised or criticised

questions.explanation: People with histrionic personality disorder are very sensitive to criticism, and often seeking out approval and reassurance.  ICD  F60.4 Histrionic personality disorder  Personality disorder characterized by:  (a)self-dramatization, theatricality, exaggerated expression of emotions;  (b)suggestibility, easily inuenced by others or by circumstances;  (c)shallow and labile a ectivity;  (d)continual seeking for excitement and activities in which the patient is the centre of attention;  (e)inappropriate seductiveness in appearance or behaviour;  (f)over-concern with physical attractiveness. Associated features may include egocentricity, self-indulgence, continuous longing for appreciation, feelings that are easily hurt, and persistent manipulative behaviour to achieve own needs.

questions.question_text: Which change to schizophrenia subtypes is true in both ICD-10 and DSM-IV?

options.text: Residual schizophrenia is no longer a feature
Paranoid schizophrenia is not a feature

questions.explanation: Simple schizophrenia was not included as a subtype in DSM-IV and was removed altogether in DSM-5.

questions.question_text: According to ICD-10, which criterion is necessary for a diagnosis of persistent delusional disorder?

options.text: Cannot be diagnosed if living with another person
Delusions present for at least one month
Can be diagnosed alongside paranoid schizophrenia

correct_answer.text: Delusions present for at least one month

correct_answers.text: Delusions present for at least one month

questions.explanation: All the others are not included in the ICD-10. The delusions are usually mood congruent. The diagnosis cannot be made alongside a  diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia or if accompanied by a dementing illness.

questions.question_text: Latah is a culturally specific syndrome in Southeast Asia. Under which ICD-10 category is it classified?
questions.explanation: Latah is classi ed under other speci ed neurotic disorders, along with many other culturally speci c syndromes.  F48.8 Other speci ed neurotic disorders:  Includes:  Briquet's disorder  Dhat syndrome  koro  latah  occupational neurosis, including writer's cramp  psychasthenia  psychasthenic neurosis  psychogenic syncope

questions.question_text: In the context of grief, the term 'incentive salience' refers to which phenomenon?

options.text: Lack of reward from pleasurable activities
Reduced interest in reminders of the deceased
Attentional bias toward objects that belonged to the deceased
Reality distortion in presence of death-related cues
Cognitive bias toward benefits of the death

correct_answer.text: Attentional bias toward objects that belonged to the deceased

correct_answers.text: Attentional bias toward objects that belonged to the deceased

questions.explanation: Why should a loss event make us feel sad universally? One explanation is o ered through the model of incentive salience for grief (Freed  and Mann, 2007). When an attachment gure dies (or leaves us), the rewarding feeling that we generally associate with the cues associated  with them persists (e.g. photographs, the daily objects that they used etc.). These cues, given their associated incentive salience,  automatically bias our attention towards them and trigger the unpleasant subjective yearning and sense of loss. This excessive attention  toward an unavailable attachment gure serves to maintain grief's core symptoms. Successfully reducing this elevated incentive salience  during separation will help one to accept the loss. Sadness that emerges during grief reaction is an adaptive coping response, which serves  to replace the association of rewarding, incentive salience with an unpleasant feeling that eventually serves to produce detachment.

questions.question_text: Dinah Mensah’s speech is: '… herbal herbal bal bal balbalbal plot … tain tain tain tain…'. What best describes this?
questions.explanation: Logoclonia is the meaningless repetition of the last syllables of words or phrases.

questions.question_text: Mr Charlesworth repeats the handshake motion 20 times but never shakes. Which phenomenon is this?
questions.explanation: Ambitendency is a phenomenon in which an individual alternates between resistance to and cooperation with instructions or prompts.   In negativism a patient resists attempts to move them and does the opposite of what is asked, seemingly without any rationale.  In Mitgehen very slight pressure on a part of the patient's body leads to movement in any direction, also called the "anglepoise" e ect or  "anglepoise lamp sign". This is done despite instructions that the patient resist the pressure. A less extreme version is termed mitmachen.   Posturing is a spontaneous and active maintenance of a posture against gravity, seemingly without purpose.   Waxy exibility (cerea exibilitas) is characterized by a patient's movements having the feeling of a plastic resistance, as if the person were  made of wax

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The negative symptoms of schizophrenia are: apathy, blunted or absent emotional responses, reduced speech, social withdrawal,  diminished attention, anhedonia, sexual problems, lethargy

questions.question_text: Which form of formal thought disorder is characterised by a lack of causal links between ideas?
questions.explanation: Asyndesis describes a lack of genuine causal links in which clusters of more or less related sequences of thoughts, instead of well-knit  sequences of thoughts are used, creating a feeling of vagueness.   Derailment is a form of thought disorder characterised by a sudden change in the train of thought and/or speech, either spontaneously or in  response to an internal stimulus, from the topic's track onto another which is obliquely related or entirely unrelated.   Metonymy involves approximate uses of words, such as paperskate rather than pen.  Fusion involves thoughts being fused together, leading to a loss of goal direction.   In drivelling there is a disordered intermixture of the constituent parts of one complex thought.

questions.question_text: Which best describes the concept of interoception?
questions.explanation: Interoception is de ned as the sense of the internal state of the body. It encompasses the brain's process of integrating signals relayed from  the allowing for a nuanced representation of the physiological state of the body. This is important for maintaining homeostatic conditions in  the body and potentially aiding in self-awareness. It is thought to be impaired in people with ASD.

questions.question_text: He insists he worked at Buckingham Palace despite evidence he did not. Which phenomenon is this?
questions.explanation: This is most likely to be a delusional memory. This is the symptom when the patient recalls as remembered an event or idea that is clearly  delusional in nature. The delusion is retrojected in time. These are sometimes called retrospective delusions.

questions.question_text: Mrs Powers recalls daily events 'like watching a video'. Which form of memory is this?
questions.explanation: Eidetic memory is the alleged ability to recall images with high detail as if they are still present.

questions.question_text: Which formal thought disorder involves interweaving two or more thoughts into one?
questions.explanation: Fusion involves thoughts being fused together, leading to a loss of goal direction.   Alogia involves a lack of unstimulated thought content, usually seen as a lack of speech.  In drivelling there is a disordered intermixture of the constituent parts of one complex thought.   A neologism describes an invented word or a known word being used to represent an under-related concept, e.g. sausage for car.   Derailment is a form of thought disorder characterised by a sudden change in the train of thought and/or speech, either spontaneously or in  response to an internal stimulus, from the topic's track onto another which is obliquely related or entirely unrelated.

questions.question_text: Miss Barlow has catatonic schizophrenia. Which of the following is an ICD-10 criterion for catatonic schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The criteria for catatonic schizophrenia are:   a. Stupor (marked decrease in reactivity to the environment and in spontaneous movements and activity) or mutism;   b. Excitement (apparently purposeless motor activity, not inuenced by external stimuli);   c. Posturing (voluntary assumption and maintenance of inappropriate or bizarre postures);   d. Negativism (an apparently motiveless resistance to all instructions or attempts to be moved, or movement in the opposite direction);   e. Rigidity (maintenance of a rigid posture against e orts to be moved);   f. Waxy exibility (maintenance of limbs and body in externally imposed positions);   g. Other symptoms such as command automatism (automatic compliance with instructions), and perseveration of words and phrases.

questions.question_text: Which method teaches a complex behaviour by breaking it into steps, each cueing the next?
questions.explanation: Chaining involves breaking a complex behaviour into steps and then teaching one step at a time, adding a new one to those that have come  before. The previous steps act as a prompt for the new one, thus building a chain.   Shaping involves giving positive reinforcement for approximations of a behaviour until it is mastering, e.g. congratulating a child for holding  a fork when they hold it by the tines rather than the handle when teaching them to use cutlery.   Prompting involves reminding a child of what they need to be doing, however this is done.  In the context of memory retrieval, cueing is achieved via prompts or cues, which include anything that is connected in some way to target  information in long-term memory, prompting retrieval of it

questions.question_text: Which of the following is one of Gestalt’s five principles of grouping?
questions.explanation: The 5 principles of Gestalt psychology are: proximity, similarity, good continuation, closure, and the law of common fate. They were  described to explain human perception of groups of objects and how we perceive parts of objects and form whole objects on the basis of  these. The concept of proximity is sometimes referred to as the principle of distance

questions.question_text: Counter-conditioning is used in which therapy?
questions.explanation: Counter-conditioning is a technique that is often employed as a part of systematic desensitisation when managing phobias and similar  disorders. It involves the conditioning of an unwanted behaviour or response to a stimulus into a wanted behaviour or response by the  association of positive actions with the stimulus. For example, when managing a phobia of dogs, a therapist may aim to associate an anxiety  provoking stimulus, such as a dog being in the next room, with a positive reward. Therefore, this will associate the positive reward with the  stimulus and diminish the anxiety associated with the latter.   Wolpe, the proponent of systematic desensitization used Guthrie's (1952) concept of counterconditioning to explain the long-term bene ts  of systematic desensitisation and claimed that desensitization replaced anxiety with relaxation.

questions.question_text: After Sergio’s phobia treatment, family also react aversively to snakes. What explains this?
questions.explanation: Stimulus preparedness posits that fear-relevant stimuli (e.g., snakes) are biologically primed to evoke fear even without learning.

questions.question_text: Which best describes the Hawthorne Effect?

options.text: Belief that one person represents the whole group
Temporary increase in work performance due to being observed
Perceiving someone as bad based on few attributes
Not helping someone in need because others are present

correct_answer.text: Temporary increase in work performance due to being observed

correct_answers.text: Temporary increase in work performance due to being observed

questions.explanation: The Hawthorne e ect describes the phenomenon of individuals or a group changing their behaviour in response to being observed.   The bystander e ect is a social psychological phenomenon in which individuals are less likely to o er help when other people are present.   The horn e ect, closely related to the halo e ect, is a form of cognitive bias that causes one's perception of another to be unduly inuenced  by a single negative trait.  The Pygmalion e ect, or Rosenthal e ect, is a psychological phenomenon wherein high expectations lead to improved performance in a  given area. The targets of the expectations internalise their positive labels, and those with positive labels succeed accordingly; a similar  process works in the opposite direction in the case of low expectations.  The group attribution error refers to people's tendency to believe either (1) that the characteristics of an individual group member are  re ective of the group as a whole, or (2) that a group's decision outcome must re ect the preferences of individual group members, even  when external information is available suggesting otherwise.

questions.question_text: You show John two word lists and ask which words appeared in both lists. What are you testing?
questions.explanation: The scenario describes one of the simplest forms of testing for recognition, which makes the retrieval process easy to record and analyse

questions.question_text: Abraham was treated with ECT. Which memory effect persists after ECT?
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia, particularly for autobiographical memory is the most persistent complication after ECT. Confusion and disorientation  usually resolves within 24-48 hours. Anterograde amnesia usually resolves within few weeks.

questions.question_text: This type of aggression is often planned and used to achieve a goal:
questions.explanation: Instrumental aggression is used with a speci c goal in mind, such as obtaining money in the course of an armed robbery.   Hostile aggression is in response to a stimulus or provocation.   Aggression can be overt and easily identi able, or covert and "passive-aggressive", e.g. bullying.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding self-serving bias?

options.text: It is a type of attribution error
It attributes internal failures to internal sources
It is a form of self-compassion
It attributes external success to external sources

correct_answer.text: It is a type of attribution error

correct_answers.text: It is a type of attribution error

questions.explanation: Self-serving bias is an attribution error where successes are internalised and failures are externalised.

questions.question_text: The tendency for a group to make riskier decisions than individuals alone is known as:
questions.explanation: Risky shift describes the phenomenon whereby a group will make more risky decisions than an individual.   This is similar to group polarisation in which a group makes more extreme decisions than the individuals would, but in terms of their initial  inclination, either cautious or risky.   Groupthink involves putting the harmony of the group foremost and avoiding disagreement at all costs, leading to an irrational decision  making process.   Conformity is the act of matching attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors to group norms.  Obedience involves a person yielding to explicit instructions or orders from an authority.

questions.question_text: Wynne and Tamara both get a C grade. Tamara blames the teacher; Wynne blames herself. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Self-serving bias is a type of cognitive bias in which positive events are attributed to one's own character, and negative events to external  factors. This can be reversed in depression.

questions.question_text: Minority influence is increased by:
questions.explanation: Minority inuence is increased by consistency in messaging, exibility, appealing to the majority view and persuading majority gureheads  to help propagate their views. If the minority is seen as being more similar to the majority, it also increases their inuence.

questions.question_text: When beliefs conflict, which is an individual most likely to do to reduce cognitive dissonance?

options.text: Seek information about the dissonant belief
Change one of their beliefs or attitudes
Emphasise the importance of the contrast

correct_answer.text: Change one of their beliefs or attitudes

correct_answers.text: Change one of their beliefs or attitudes

questions.explanation: Individuals experiencing cognitive dissonance can resolve this by:  Changing behaviours  Changing beliefs or attitudes to reduce the dissonance  Reduce the importance of the dissonance   Ignore information that emphasises the dissonance  Of these, changing behaviours is the least likely to occur. Individuals do not tend to acknowledge the dissonance explicitly as this would  involve recognising that their thoughts are contradictory, which is psychologically threatening. They are most likely to change their beliefs or  attitudes to reduce the dissonance

questions.question_text: The phenomenon whereby individuals are less likely to help when others are present is called:
questions.explanation: Diffusion of responsibility occurs when presence of others reduces a person’s sense of personal obligation to act.

questions.question_text: Asch found that which factor leads to group disintegration (less conformity)?
questions.explanation: Asch theorised that group conformity was more likely with larger numbers, more challenging tasks, conversations being more public and  individuals perceiving other members as being more senior than them.

questions.question_text: Social pressure in groups: what increases an individual’s likelihood of expressing ambivalence?

options.text: Feels less identified with the group
Need to appear part of the group

correct_answer.text: Feels less identified with the group

correct_answers.text: Feels less identified with the group

questions.explanation: A lesser degree of identi cation with a given group increases the likelihood an individual will express ambivalence or a dissenting opinion.

questions.question_text: Jennifer is 12 and seeking peer approval. According to Kohlberg, she is at which moral stage?
questions.explanation: She is likely in the conventional stage of interpersonal accord and conformity, or the good boy/girl orientation whereby individuals conform  to social standards and are receptive to approval or disapproval from others as it re ects society's views. They try to be a "good boy" or  "good girl" to live up to these expectations having learned that being regarded as good bene ts the self.

questions.question_text: Which is true about ethnic differences in UK mental healthcare access?

options.text: Cultural competence of providers does not affect access
Most ethnic minorities receive care via GPs
Psychotic disorders are less often diagnosed in black men
Anxiety and depression are highest among white women
Black and South Asian individuals are less likely to obtain mental healthcare

correct_answer.text: Black and South Asian individuals are less likely to obtain mental healthcare

correct_answers.text: Black and South Asian individuals are less likely to obtain mental healthcare

questions.explanation: Among BME communities, mental illnesses are more prevalent but less treated.   There is relatively higher prevalence of anxiety and depression in South Asian women (63.5% compared with 28.5% of white women), and  psychotic disorders in Afro-Caribbean men (3.1% compared with 0.2% of white men).   In general, people from ethnic minorities are less likely than their White British counterparts to have contacted their GP about mental health  issues in the last year, to be prescribed antidepressants, or to be referred to specialist mental health services. There is some evidence that  hard-to-reach groups, including BME, are less likely to obtain appropriate mental healthcare and may be disadvantaged either because they  are unable to access services or because they receive inadequate help from services.   Factors considered important barriers to accessing services include cultural competence (i.e. the ability of providers and organisations to  e ectively deliver healthcare services that meet the social, cultural and linguistic needs of patients); cultural models of illness; stigma; fear  and perceived discrimination and barriers to communication

questions.question_text: Mr Daio accuses his wife of witchcraft and tries to exorcise demons from her. Which culture-bound syndrome best fits?
questions.explanation: Bou ée délirante describes sudden attacks of brief duration with paranoid delusions and often concomitant hallucinations, typically  precipitated by an intense fear of magical persecution through sorcery or witchcraft. It is a syndrome occurring in Francophone West Africa  and Haiti.  Ataque de nervios translates as "attack of nerves" and is commonly associated with Hispanic populations, with symptoms including  uncontrollable screaming or shouting, crying, trembling, sensations of heat rising in the chest and head, dissociative experiences, and verbal  or physical aggression. The reaction is usually associated with a stressful event relating to the family.   Koro is a culture-speci c syndrome delusional disorder in which an individual has an overpowering belief that one's genitalia are retracting  and will disappear, despite the lack of any true longstanding changes to the genitals. It is more associated with Asian populations but there  have been epidemics in Africa, the US and Europe. Latah is most commonly seen in Southeast Asia and is characterised by abnormal behaviors result from a person experiencing a suddenshock. The a ected person typically engages in such behaviours as screaming, cursing, dancing type movements, and uncontrollablelaughter, and will typically mimic the words or actions of those around them. Brain fag is commonly seen in West African students and is characterised by symptoms including somatic, sleep-related and cognitivecomplaints, head and neck pains, di culty in concentrating and retaining information, and eye pain. It is thought to be related to stress fromstudying.

questions.question_text: Which term describes social disadvantage as a result of disability?
questions.explanation: Handicap is the social disadvantage resulting from disability.   Enacted stigma (external stigma, discrimination) refers to the experience of unfair treatment by others.   Felt stigma (internal stigma or self-stigmatization) refers to the shame and expectation of discrimination that prevents people from talking  about their experiences and stops them seeking help.

questions.question_text: Which is FALSE about high expressed emotion (EE) in families of schizophrenia patients?

options.text: Males have higher relapse risk than females under high EE
Criticism, emotional over-involvement, and hostility predict relapse
Over 50% of carers show high EE
EE is measured by the Camberwell Family Interview

correct_answer.text: Males have higher relapse risk than females under high EE

correct_answers.text: Males have higher relapse risk than females under high EE

questions.explanation: There is no evidence of a gender difference in relapse risk under high EE; both sexes are equally affected.

questions.question_text: Mr Khan is fluent in Kashmiri at home and in English with colleagues. This acculturation pattern is called:
questions.explanation: Cultural integration is a form of cultural exchange in which one group assumes the beliefs, practices and rituals of another group without  sacri cing the characteristics of its own culture.   Cultural assimilation occurs when members of a minority group become indistinguishable from the dominant group.   Acculturation refers to the socialisation process by which foreign-born individuals adopt the values, customs, norms, attitudes, and  behaviours of the dominant host culture.   Enculturation is the process by which people learn the dynamics of their surrounding culture and acquire values and norms appropriate or  necessary in that culture and worldviews.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT true about Kohlberg’s theory of moral development?

options.text: Individuals can show more than one stage at a time
The stages are not culturally neutral
Conventional stages compare actions with society’s views

questions.explanation: All adults do not reach the post-conventional stages of moral development. At the same time, people in di erent cultures seem to move  through the sequence at di erent rates and to reach di erent end-points. Edwards et al., in 1980, reported that in the West, most urban  middle-class adults reach stage 4 (conventional), with a small percentage using some stage 5 (post-conventional) reasoning. In the isolated  villages and tribal communities of many countries, however, it is rare to nd any adult beyond stage 3.

questions.question_text: Which defence mechanisms are most common in patients with anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Denial, rationalisation and intellectualisation are commonly seen in patients with anorexia nervosa.

questions.question_text: Mr Davies explains his wife’s delusional ideas in a calm, matter-of-fact way. This defence mechanism is:
questions.explanation: Intellectualisation is a form of defence mechanism where an individual concentrates on the intellectual components of a situation so as to  distance oneself from the associated anxiety-provoking emotions.  Rationalisation is a defence mechanism where the individual devises reassuring or self-serving but incorrect explanations for his or her own  or others' thoughts, actions, or feelings.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT a Kleinian defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Isolation is not a Kleinian defence. It is characterised as a mental process involving the creation of a gap between an unpleasant or  threatening cognition, and other thoughts and feelings. By minimising associative connections with other thoughts, the threatening  cognition is remembered less often and is less likely to a ect self-esteem or the self-concept. The other defences listed are more primitive  and were addressed more by Klein in her work with children.

questions.question_text: Which defence is known as the 'primary defence' in psychoanalytic theory?
questions.explanation: Repression has been referred to the Primary Defence for the unconscious as it involves preventing thoughts or impulses becoming  conscious.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a mature defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Suppression is the conscious decision to postpone attention to distressing thoughts and is a mature defence.

questions.question_text: According to Freud’s dual instinct theory, which instinct is the death instinct?
questions.explanation: Dual instinct theory looks at Eros and Thanatos as life and death instincts. Freud believed that Thanatos underlay and accompanied Eros  and so could be seen as more primal

questions.question_text: Sam cleans his room without being asked after an argument with his mother. Which defence is this?
questions.explanation: In undoing an individual tries to “undo" an unhealthy, destructive or otherwise threatening thought by acting out the reverse of the  unacceptable. It involves symbolically nullifying an unacceptable or guilt provoking thought, idea, or feeling by confession or atonement.

questions.question_text: Some animals demonstrate the phenomenon of perceiving the first moving object they see after birth as being their mother. Which of the following best describes this?
questions.explanation: This describes lial imprinting that is often seen in birds. Newly hatched chicks will identify an object seen after birth as their mother and  follow it persistently. This tends to occur within a certain critical time period shortly after hatching. More generally, imprinting is any kind of  phase-sensitive learning (learning occurring at a particular age or a particular life stage) that is rapid and apparently independent of the  consequences of behaviour.   The Westermark e ect is seen in instances where two people who live in domestic proximity during the rst few years in the life of either  one become desensitised to later close sexual attraction.   Classical conditioning refers to a learning procedure in which a biologically potent stimulus (e.g. food) is paired with a previously neutral  stimulus (e.g. a bell).   In classical conditioning, stimulus generalisation is said to occur if, after a particular conditioned stimulus has come to elicit a response,  another similar stimulus will elicit the same response.
